Packages: `rugarch`, `FinTS`, `yaml`, `xts` (installation: `Rscript R/install_packages.R`).

This notebook repeats with `rugarch` the steps of `notebooks/python/05_garch.ipynb` (package `arch`), on the same percent returns and the same training sample. It then compares the results with the files written by Python, so the Python notebook must be run **first**.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Resolve the project root once so every path below is relative to it, whatever folder knitr runs in.
ROOT <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE), winslash = "/"))
while (!file.exists(file.path(ROOT, "config.yaml"))) ROOT <- dirname(ROOT)
source(file.path(ROOT, "R", "load_data.R"))
source(file.path(ROOT, "R", "arima_helpers.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(rugarch))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = ROOT)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "", fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5)
cfg <- load_config(ROOT)
set.seed(cfg$seed)  # same seed as Python
RES <- file.path(ROOT, cfg$paths$results)
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.2g", x)
```

## 0. Data

```{r data}
# Percent returns, same train end as Python (config.yaml); pivot for the pre / post fits.
panel <- load_panel(ROOT)
S <- c("CONVERTS", "PURE", "BTC", "NVDA")
r <- 100 * na.omit(panel[, paste0(S, "_log_return")]); colnames(r) <- S
r_tr <- r[paste0("/", cfg$split$train_end)]
piv <- as.Date(cfg$pivot_date)
cat("train returns:", nrow(r_tr), "| all returns:", nrow(r), "\n")
```

## 1. ARCH-LM on the ARIMA(0,1,0) residuals

```{r archlm}
# ARIMA(0,1,0) residuals = returns (no drift), as in Phase 3; FinTS::ArchTest with m = 5 and 10.
al <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("CONVERTS", "PURE"), function(s) do.call(rbind, lapply(c(5, 10), function(m) {
  a <- FinTS::ArchTest(as.numeric(r_tr[, s]) / 100, lags = m)
  data.frame(series = s, lag = m, LM = unname(a$statistic), p_value = a$p.value)
}))))
al$conclusion <- ifelse(al$p_value < 0.05, "reject H0 (ARCH effect)", "H0 not rejected")
al
```

Same conclusion as in Python: there is no ARCH effect for CONVERTS (p = `r round(al$p_value[al$series == "CONVERTS" & al$lag == 5], 3)` at lag 5) and one is present for PURE (p = `r signif(al$p_value[al$series == "PURE" & al$lag == 5], 3)`).

## 2. Model comparison on CONVERTS (training sample)

```{r fit}
# Same four specifications as Python: constant mean, Student-t ("std") or normal errors; solver "hybrid" for robustness.
mk <- function(model, dist, sub = NULL) ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model = model, garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE), distribution.model = dist)
specs <- list("GARCH(1,1)-N" = mk("sGARCH", "norm"), "GARCH(1,1)-t" = mk("sGARCH", "std"),
              "GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t" = mk("gjrGARCH", "std"), "EGARCH(1,1)-t" = mk("eGARCH", "std"))
x <- as.numeric(r_tr[, "CONVERTS"])
fits <- lapply(specs, function(sp) ugarchfit(sp, x, solver = "hybrid"))
comp_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(n) {
  f <- fits[[n]]; ic <- infocriteria(f)
  data.frame(model = n, loglik = likelihood(f), AIC_per_obs = ic["Akaike", 1], BIC_per_obs = ic["Bayes", 1],
             persistence = persistence(f), half_life = halflife(f))
}))
write.csv(comp_r, file.path(RES, "05_garch_comparison_r.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
comp_r
```

`rugarch` divides AIC and BIC by the number of observations. The ranking is the same as in the Python table, but the values cannot be compared directly.

```{r compare}
# Parameter-by-parameter comparison with Python for the two models whose parameterisation is identical (GARCH, GJR).
py <- read.csv(file.path(RES, "05_garch_python_params.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
map <- c("mu" = "mu", "omega" = "omega", "alpha[1]" = "alpha1", "beta[1]" = "beta1", "gamma[1]" = "gamma1", "nu" = "shape")
rows <- list()
for (n in c("GARCH(1,1)-N", "GARCH(1,1)-t", "GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t")) {
  cf <- coef(fits[[n]]); p <- py[py$model == n, ]
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(p))) {
    rn <- map[[p$parameter[k]]]
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(model = n, parameter = p$parameter[k], python = p$estimate[k], R = unname(cf[rn]),
                                           loglik_python = p$loglik[k], loglik_R = likelihood(fits[[n]]))
  }
}
pcmp <- do.call(rbind, rows)
pcmp$abs_diff <- abs(pcmp$R - pcmp$python)
write.csv(pcmp, file.path(RES, "05_python_vs_r_params.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
pcmp
```

**Reading.**

* **GARCH(1,1) and GJR-GARCH(1,1): close, not identical.**
  * The maximum difference on the persistence α + β is `r fmt(max(abs((pcmp$R[pcmp$parameter=="alpha[1]"] + pcmp$R[pcmp$parameter=="beta[1]"]) - (pcmp$python[pcmp$parameter=="alpha[1]"] + pcmp$python[pcmp$parameter=="beta[1]"]))))`.
  * Python reaches a slightly **higher** log-likelihood (maximum difference `r fmt(max(abs(pcmp$loglik_R - pcmp$loglik_python)))`): rugarch's optimiser stops slightly before the optimum.
  * ω varies the most, which is expected: when α is almost zero, ω and β offset each other and are poorly separated.
* **Very weak reaction to shocks for CONVERTS.** The α of the GARCH(1,1)-t is `r round(coef(fits[["GARCH(1,1)-t"]])["alpha1"], 4)` in R, against a memory β of `r round(coef(fits[["GARCH(1,1)-t"]])["beta1"], 4)`. Volatility reacts very little to shocks, as in Python.

```{r egarch}
# EGARCH: rugarch's alpha1 is the SIGN effect and gamma1 the SIZE effect (the reverse of arch's naming).
round(cbind(estimate = coef(fits[["EGARCH(1,1)-t"]]), se = fits[["EGARCH(1,1)-t"]]@fit$matcoef[, 2]), 4)
```

**EGARCH.** The parameterisation of `rugarch` differs from that of `arch`:
* in `rugarch`, the size effect is called gamma1; here it is `r round(coef(fits[["EGARCH(1,1)-t"]])["gamma1"], 4)`;
* in `arch`, it is called α, and Python estimates it at −0.0523.

Log-likelihood: `r round(likelihood(fits[["EGARCH(1,1)-t"]]), 2)` in R, vs −3,573.19 in Python. **Comparing the two packages works as a test**, and it is instructive.

* **R finds a regular solution**: positive size effect (`r round(coef(fits[["EGARCH(1,1)-t"]])["gamma1"], 4)`), non-significant sign effect, persistence `r round(persistence(fits[["EGARCH(1,1)-t"]]), 3)`, normal standard errors. Its log-likelihood is practically equal to that of the GARCH(1,1)-t in R (`r round(likelihood(fits[["GARCH(1,1)-t"]]), 2)`): the EGARCH adds nothing.
* **Python finds a higher likelihood**, but with a negative size effect, near-zero standard errors and a forecast variance that collapses. This is a **degenerate solution**, not a better model.

**Conclusion:** the "best AIC" of the EGARCH in the Python notebook is an **optimisation artefact**. It should be disregarded.

## 3. Standardised residual diagnostics (GARCH(1,1)-t)

```{r diag}
# Same tests as Python on z = residual / sigma: Ljung-Box on z and z², ARCH-LM on z.
dz <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("CONVERTS", "PURE", "BTC"), function(s) {
  f <- ugarchfit(specs[["GARCH(1,1)-t"]], as.numeric(r_tr[, s]), solver = "hybrid")
  z <- as.numeric(residuals(f, standardize = TRUE))
  data.frame(series = s,
             LB_z_10 = Box.test(z, 10, "Ljung-Box")$p.value, LB_z2_10 = Box.test(z^2, 10, "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
             ARCH_z_5 = FinTS::ArchTest(z, lags = 5)$p.value, nu = unname(coef(f)["shape"]))
}))
dz
```

For all three series, no autocorrelation or ARCH effect remains in the standardised residuals: all p-values are ≥ `r round(min(dz[, 2:4]), 3)`. This matches the Python conclusions.

## 4. Persistence before / after the pivot

```{r prepost}
# GARCH(1,1)-t on each regime (all observations of the regime), as in Python section 5.
pp_r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(S, function(s) do.call(rbind, lapply(c("pre-pivot", "post-pivot"), function(lab) {
  d <- zoo::index(r); xx <- as.numeric(r[if (lab == "pre-pivot") d < piv else d >= piv, s])
  f <- tryCatch(ugarchfit(specs[["GARCH(1,1)-t"]], xx, solver = "hybrid"), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(f) || f@fit$convergence != 0) return(data.frame(series = s, period = lab, n = length(xx), alpha = NA, beta = NA, persistence = NA, se_beta = NA))
  mc <- f@fit$matcoef
  data.frame(series = s, period = lab, n = length(xx), alpha = mc["alpha1", 1], beta = mc["beta1", 1],
             persistence = persistence(f), se_beta = mc["beta1", 2])
}))))
py_pp <- read.csv(file.path(RES, "05_persistence_pre_post.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
pp_r$persistence_python <- py_pp$persistence
pp_r$identified_python <- py_pp$identified
write.csv(pp_r, file.path(RES, "05_persistence_pre_post_r.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
pp_r
```

**Reading.**

* **Before the pivot**, R and Python give close persistence values for all four series.
* **After the pivot**, the estimates for CONVERTS, PURE and BTC are **poorly identified** in both packages: the standard error of β is of the same order as β, or the optimiser ends at different values. With 447 observations, comparing persistence after the pivot therefore makes no sense for these series. Only NVDA remains well estimated.

## 5. Variance forecast from the first origin

```{r fcst}
# 10-day variance forecast from the last train day, compared with Python's garch_t forecast at the same origin.
f <- fits[["GARCH(1,1)-t"]]
fr <- as.numeric(sigma(ugarchforecast(f, n.ahead = 10)))^2
pyf <- read.csv(file.path(RES, "forecasts_garch_vol.csv"))
pyf <- pyf[pyf$series == "CONVERTS" & pyf$model == "garch_t" & pyf$origin == cfg$split$train_end, ]
fc <- data.frame(horizon = 1:10, variance_R = fr, variance_Py = pyf$y_pred[order(pyf$horizon)])
fc$reldiff <- abs(fc$variance_R / fc$variance_Py - 1)
write.csv(fc, file.path(RES, "05_vol_forecast_first_origin_r_vs_python.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
fc
```

Maximum relative difference on the forecast variance: `r fmt(max(fc$reldiff))`.

## Conclusion of the comparison

**Points of agreement between R (`rugarch`) and Python (`arch`):**
* ARCH-LM: no effect for CONVERTS, effect present for PURE;
* GARCH and GJR close (Python reaches a slightly better optimum);
* clean standardised residuals;
* persistence well identified before the pivot, poorly identified after (except NVDA);
* very close variance forecasts.

**Point of disagreement: the EGARCH.** Python's solution is degenerate, R's is regular, and the latter does not improve on the GARCH(1,1)-t. This confirms the choice of GARCH(1,1)-t. The other differences come from the optimiser.
